name: Pyridoxamine
lead: Pyridoxamine is one of the three natural forms of vitamin B6. Its chemistry allows it to scavenge free radicals and reactive carbonyl compounds and to chelate metal ions [1]. It is discussed in longevity and skin circles as an inhibitor of advanced glycation end products (AGEs), compounds linked in the literature to diabetic complications and tissue ageing [1][2].

Most research on it concerns diabetic kidney disease, where it was developed by Biostratum and later NephroGenex as the drug candidate Pyridorin [1]. Animal studies reported protection of kidney and retina in diabetic rats [3][4]. Its status in the United States is unusual: in 2009 the FDA ruled that pyridoxamine products fall outside the legal definition of a dietary supplement [1]. No study found examines pyridoxamine for skin appearance.
infobox: FDA ruled in 2009 that it is not a dietary supplement [1]

paras: Pyridoxamine differs from pyridoxine at the 4-position of the pyridine ring [1]. It is reported to inhibit the Maillard reaction and the formation of AGEs, possibly by trapping Amadori intermediates and interrupting metal-dependent steps in their breakdown, and also to inhibit advanced lipoxidation end products [1]. In diabetic animal models it improved kidney histology about as well as or better than aminoguanidine [1]. Reviews of glycoxidation and lipoxidation describe these processes as involved in atherosclerosis and diabetic complications [5][6].

Biostratum developed pyridoxamine as Pyridorin for diabetic nephropathy; Wikipedia reports that funding ran out in 2005 before a Phase III trial began [1]. Biostratum filed a citizen petition in 2005 arguing that pyridoxamine was an investigational drug and should not be sold as a supplement [1]. NephroGenex licensed Pyridorin in 2006, restarted development in 2008, began a Phase 3 study and ended it in 2016 for lack of funding; the company filed for bankruptcy that year [1]. In January 2009 the FDA ruled that pyridoxamine products are outside the supplement definition of the 1994 DSHEA law, reasoning that its earlier investigational status meant independent evidence of prior supplement use was required [1].

ClinicalTrials.gov lists Phase 2 trials of Pyridorin in diabetic nephropathy (registered starts 2001, 2002 and 2008, the last with 317 participants) [7][8][9], and a Phase 3 trial begun in 2014 that was terminated [10]. Wikipedia reports that a Phase II trial of 224 patients suggested slowed disease progression [1]. Other registered studies examined pyridoxamine supplementation on vascular function and insulin sensitivity in abdominal obesity [11], on bone material strength in type 2 diabetes [12], and on microvascular function in type 2 diabetes [13]; a trial for kidney stones was withdrawn [14].
No studies found that test pyridoxamine for skin appearance or facial ageing. Animal work showed effects against early renal disease and dyslipidemia and against retinopathy in diabetic rats [3][4].

card.summary: A vitamin B6 form studied as an AGE inhibitor in diabetic kidney disease, with no appearance research.
card.note: The FDA ruled in 2009 it is not a legal dietary supplement in the US.

quick.overview:
Pyridoxamine is a natural form of vitamin B6 that is discussed as an inhibitor of advanced glycation end products, which are linked to tissue ageing and diabetic complications.

Its clinical development was for diabetic kidney disease and ended in 2016 when the sponsor ran out of funding. No study found tests it for skin or looks.
quick.mechanism: It is reported to trap reactive carbonyl intermediates, chelate metals and scavenge radicals, thereby limiting glycation and lipoxidation products.
quick.risks: Safety data are not detailed in the sources reviewed. In the US the FDA ruled in 2009 that pyridoxamine products are not dietary supplements under DSHEA.
